theme: The rich man and Lazarus; faith; the coming kingdom
readingInstruction: Read Luke 16:1-17:37. A shrewd manager, the rich man and Lazarus, warnings about stumbling, forgiveness, faith, ten lepers, and the coming of the kingdom. These are hard sayings. Read slowly.
settingTheScene: On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus continues to teach the disciples while the Pharisees, who love money, listen and scoff. His teaching in these chapters keeps coming back to money, faithfulness, and readiness for the kingdom. Luke 16 is the most pointed teaching on wealth in the Gospels.
observation: “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much” (16:10).
“Son, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things” (16:25).
“If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead” (16:31).
“If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed” (17:6).
“Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine?” (17:17).
“For behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you” (17:21).
interpretation:
The parable of the shrewd manager is puzzling. A manager, about to be fired, reduces the debts of his master’s debtors to make friends. The master commends his shrewdness. Jesus does not praise dishonesty. The point is that the people of this age plan ahead for their future, so the children of light should use worldly wealth with an eye to eternity. “Make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth.” Money is a tool, not a master: “You cannot serve God and money.” The Pharisees sneer, and Jesus tells them that what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.

Then comes the rich man and Lazarus. A rich man dresses in purple and feasts daily, while a beggar named Lazarus lies at his gate covered with sores. Both die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham’s side, and the rich man is in torment. This is the only parable in which a character has a name, and he is the poor one. The rich man asks Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his brothers. Abraham answers, “They have Moses and the Prophets.” If they do not listen to Scripture, they will not be convinced even by one who rises from the dead. The story is a warning about hardened hearts, and an irony: someone did rise from the dead, and many did not believe.

Chapter 17 begins with a warning about causing little ones to stumble, and a call to forgive repeatedly. The apostles say, “Increase our faith!” Jesus replies that faith the size of a mustard seed can do surprising things. It is not the quantity but the object that matters. Then he tells them that servants who have done all that was commanded say, “We are unworthy servants.”

Ten lepers are healed, and only one returns to give thanks, a Samaritan. Jesus says, “Your faith has made you well.” Then the Pharisees ask when the kingdom will come, and Jesus replies, “The kingdom of God is in the midst of you.” The King is standing among them. He then speaks of the days of the Son of Man, which will come suddenly like lightning, and warns, “Remember Lot’s wife.”
connection: Deuteronomy 15:7-11 commands generosity toward the poor. Proverbs 14:31 says whoever oppresses the poor shows contempt for his Maker. Isaiah 8:19-20 sends people to the law and the testimony. Matthew 6:24 has the same saying about two masters. Luke 24:25-27 returns to the importance of Moses and the Prophets. 1 Timothy 6:17-19 gives instructions to the rich. 2 Kings 5 recounts the healing of Naaman, the leper who was a foreigner. 1 Thessalonians 5:18 says to give thanks in all circumstances.
application:
Look at your own giving and spending. Are you using money as a tool for eternity?

Be the one leper who returns. Write a thank you note to God or to someone who has helped you.

Read your Bible faithfully. Moses and the Prophets still speak.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you are tempted to serve besides him, such as money.
Ask him to open your eyes to the “Lazarus” at your gate.
Ask him to teach you to be faithful in little.
